title: Fully remote with no associates: Meet the 'elite' law firm of the future
author: Maria Ward-Brennan

dom.t: Law-firm pyramid: Efficiency threatens revenue and training

st.t: Law-firm pyramid: Efficiency threatens revenue and training
st.an: Provides a concrete case of the structural shift described by the cluster: Pierson Ferdinand largely substitutes generative AI for associate drafting, concentrates work among partners and uses a limited junior-partner shadowing programme instead of a conventional associate pyramid. This materially illustrates both reduced leverage and an alternative training model, though its productivity and pricing claims are not independently measured.
qs: ## AI over Associates  At Pierson Ferdinand, the firm has fully embraced technology, largely replacing associates with GenAI through platforms like Harvey AI.

st.t: Service model: AI challenges production more than lawyers
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core proposition and supplies a concrete law-firm model built around it: GenAI replaces much junior drafting while partners retain higher-level legal work, and a junior-partner programme provides deliberate professional development despite minimal associate staffing. Its claims are company-reported rather than independent evidence of market-wide viability.
qs: "What this really does is enable our partners to execute at a really high level because a lot of the first drafts of anything that would normally be done by junior staff can now largely be replaced by GenAI," Pierson explained.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s work-redesign thesis and materially extends it with a concrete operating-model example: a full-service, remote firm that has removed associates, uses generative AI including Harvey for much associate work, and has rapidly expanded its partner base. It supports structural pressure on junior work and traditional leverage, though it does not provide task-level evidence on capability, verification or realised productivity.
qs: ## AI over Associates  At Pierson Ferdinand, the firm has fully embraced technology, largely replacing associates with GenAI through platforms like Harvey AI.
In just under two years, the firm has grown to over 260 partners across 26 locations, including its first non-US office in London, which opened last July.

st.t: Associate training: Automation threatens expertise reproduction
st.an: The source provides a concrete operational example of the cluster’s core concern: GenAI replaces junior first-draft work, while the firm largely bypasses a broad associate training pipeline and develops only selected fifth-year lawyers through partner shadowing. It supports the claimed threat to expertise reproduction, although it does not directly examine whether those lawyers will lack the experience needed to verify AI output.
qs: "What this really does is enable our partners to execute at a really high level because a lot of the first drafts of anything that would normally be done by junior staff can now largely be replaced by GenAI," Pierson explained.
"We have the ability to provide the depth and breadth of legal practice that we would need without having to train the associates on our clients' pound," he added.

kp.k: Partner-led, technology-focused firm reports rapid expansion
kp.d: The article reports that New York-based Pierson Ferdinand launched in January 2024 with over 130 partners, mostly from FisherBroyles, and grew to over 260 partners across 26 locations in just under two years. Its first non-US office opened in London last July. Michael Pierson frames the model as a response to remote working, an ageing workforce and GenAI, looking ahead to big law in 10 years rather than reporting a sector-wide transformation.
qs: Founded in January 2024, New York-based Pierson Ferdinand became the largest law firm launch in the US, with over 130 partners joining, most of whom came from FisherBroyles, where Pierson and Ferdinand were senior partners.
In just under two years, the firm has grown to over 260 partners across 26 locations, including its first non-US office in London, which opened last July.
What is the future of big law going to look like in 10 years' time, given what we know about remote working culture, an ageing workforce and Gen AI

kp.k: GenAI substitutes for junior drafting in partner-led delivery
kp.d: The article describes the firm as largely replacing associates with GenAI through platforms such as Harvey AI. Pierson says first drafts normally produced by junior staff can largely be replaced, enabling partners to focus on high-level work and offer competitively priced services without charging clients for associate training. These are Pierson's operational and commercial claims; the article supplies no measured productivity or pricing comparison. Despite the headline, the firm has a couple of associates in London, attributed largely to cultural differences, and none in the US.
qs: At Pierson Ferdinand, the firm has fully embraced technology, largely replacing associates with GenAI through platforms like Harvey AI.

What this really does is enable our partners to execute at a really high level because a lot of the first drafts of anything that would normally be done by junior staff can now largely be replaced by GenAI,
The firm has a couple of associates in its London office but, largely due to cultural differences, it has none in the US.
We have the ability to provide the depth and breadth of legal practice that we would need without having to train the associates on our clients' pound,

kp.k: Junior partner programme provides a distinct development pathway
kp.d: The article reports around a dozen participants in a junior partner programme for top lawyers in their fifth year identified as future full partners. Pierson describes shadowing senior lawyers to learn case and client-matter management, invoicing and team development, preserving a development route within the firm's largely associate-free structure.
qs: The firm has around a dozen on its 'junior partner' programme, for top lawyers who are in their fifth year and were identified as future full law firm partners.
They join as a junior partner, and they shadow some of the more senior people, and learn what it is to manage the cases, client matters, invoicing process and developing a team.

kp.k: Associate salary competition coexists with AI employment uncertainty
kp.d: Ward-Brennan places the firm's approach against rising newly qualified lawyer salaries in the City, with top English firms trying to match American compensation, and substantial sector investment in AI. She characterises the discussion of AI's implications for junior jobs as muted and uncertain, not as evidence of established sector-wide job losses.
qs: This comes as the pay war over associates continues to intensify, with law firms in the City competing to outdo each other in pushing up salaries for their most junior lawyers, newly qualified (NQ), a trend that has seen many top English firms trying to match the compensation offered by their American counterparts.
On top of this, as every top law firm pours money into AI tools, the scepticism over what this will mean for jobs, especially junior roles, has been slowly whispered in the background.

kp.k: Remote operations reduce overhead and support partner recruitment
kp.d: The firm operates remotely without US office space, while retaining a serviced London office for client meetings. Pierson opposes compulsory five-day office attendance and says substantial operational savings allow most profit to pass to partners, forming a recruitment proposition. He also argues that technology-enabled growth can improve stressed lawyers' lives; these benefits are presented as his claims rather than quantified findings.
qs: The firm has no office space in the US, but it maintains a serviced office for its London partners at One King William Street, used for client meetings.
We think it's a mistake to say that everyone needs to be back in the office five days a week, because clearly the workers don't want it,

By reducing operational costs for law firms substantially and passing most of the profit to our partners, we can make a positive impact. That's really, I think, the compelling value prop to the partners who are joining us,

kp.k: Transparent compensation rewards origination, production and recruitment
kp.d: Pierson describes an algorithmic compensation system based on origination, working-attorney production and recruitment credit. He says everyone in the firm can see matter origination, work production, client invoice payment, expense deductions and colleagues' compensation. The article presents this remuneration design alongside technology, low associate numbers and remote working as elements of the firm's economic model.
qs: which is based on a very simple formula that awards origination credit, working attorney credit, which you call production credit, and then recruitment credit at the firm.

It is a fully transparent system where anyone can see who originated a matter, who produced, when the last time the client paid the invoice, and how the expenses were deducted, and of course, everyone's compensation is visible to everyone in the firm,

kp.k: Partners choose billable hours without mandatory targets
kp.d: The article frames AI adoption as pressure to rethink client charging and reports Pierson's dissatisfaction with the current system. Its concrete description is that partners choose how many hours to bill, with the compensation algorithm rewarding high performers while accommodating lower hours; it does not specify a replacement client-pricing arrangement.
qs: At a time when the hourly billing system at law firms is uncertain, the adoption of AI is putting pressure on lawyers to rethink their charging methods for clients.
At Pierson Ferdinand, partners don't have mandatory hourly billable targets, as each partner can decide how many hours to bill.
High performers are rewarded, but those who prefer fewer billable hours are also accommodated, due to the firm's compensation algorithm.

kp.k: Pierson links flexibility to female partner representation
kp.d: Pierson suggests the firm's remote working and billing flexibility have contributed to workforce diversity. The article reports 40 per cent female partners against an average English law firm figure of 37 per cent. The causal link is his suggestion, not a demonstrated finding.
qs: He suggested that the firm's approach to remote working, along with partners not being bound by hourly billable rates, has led to a diverse workforce, including 40 per cent female partners, above the average English law firm, which stands at 37 per cent.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Pierson says generative AI can largely replace junior lawyers' first-draft work, enabling a predominantly partner-only firm to deliver high-level services at competitive prices.
pts.d: Ward-Brennan reports that Pierson Ferdinand largely replaces associates with generative AI through platforms including Harvey AI. Michael Pierson explains that replacing junior drafting work lets partners focus on higher-level work and avoids charging clients for associate training. The reported model has no US associates but retains a couple in London; it is not a claim that AI autonomously supplies all legal services or replaces partners.

pts.k: The article presents AI as a source of uncertainty for junior legal employment and pressure on hourly charging.
pts.d: Ward-Brennan links firms' AI investment to questions about future junior staffing and states that AI adoption is pressing lawyers to reconsider client charging methods. She reports Pierson's view that the current billing system is not attainable. Pierson Ferdinand's concrete practice is to dispense with mandatory billable-hour targets, not an explicitly documented abandonment of hourly billing or adoption of fixed fees. The article supplies no quantified sector-wide displacement prediction.

pts.k: Pierson presents technology-enabled, remote, low-associate practice as a lower-cost model that can improve partners' economics and working lives.
pts.d: Ward-Brennan attributes the combination of technology, remote working and few or no associates to bottom-line considerations. Pierson says technology-enabled growth can improve lawyers' lives and that substantially reduced operating costs allow most profit to pass to partners. These are claims about the combined organisational model: the source does not isolate AI's contribution from office savings, compensation arrangements or other technology.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence offered is a reported firm case study and its co-founder's account, with staffing and growth figures rather than measured AI performance or savings.
pts.d: The article reports a January 2024 launch with more than 130 partners, growth to more than 260 across 26 locations in under two years, and the US/London associate distinction. It also reports approximately a dozen fifth-year lawyers in a junior-partner programme, showing an alternative development route rather than the elimination of all less-senior lawyers. These facts contextualise Pierson's account but do not separately measure AI's effects. No drafting benchmarks, client-price comparisons, quantified operating savings, output-quality measures or sector-wide employment data are supplied.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: AI drafting substitution is described as already occurring in 2025; the firm's strategic framing looks ten years ahead without a dated industry-wide replacement forecast.
pts.d: Pierson's claim concerns what generative AI can 'now' largely replace, specifically first drafts ordinarily produced by junior staff. The business began in January 2024 and is presented in the 2025 article as an operating model. Pierson describes planning around a ten-year view of Big Law conditioned on generative AI, remote-working culture and an ageing workforce. The source gives no timetable for broader junior-job losses or replacement of hourly charging, and qualifies the associate-free description with London's exceptions.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The claimed effects concern junior lawyers' work and employment prospects, partners' work and remuneration, clients' prices, and competing full-service firms' staffing and billing models.
pts.d: Junior associates are the principal role whose first-draft tasks are said to be substituted. Partners remain responsible for executing higher-level work and are presented as beneficiaries of lower overheads and flexible billable-hour targets. Clients are said to receive competitively priced services without paying for associate training. A small junior-partner cohort learns case management and business responsibilities through shadowing. The broader discussion concerns Big Law and leading City firms investing in AI, not a quantified claim about all lawyers or access to justice.
